In this exercise, we use tidyverse (ggplot2, dplyr, etc) to explore the MIMIC-IV data introduced in homework 1 and to build a cohort of ICU stays.

Q1. Visualizing patient trajectory

Visualizing a patient’s encounters in a health care system is a common task in clinical data analysis. In this question, we will visualize a patient’s ADT (admission-discharge-transfer) history and ICU vitals in the MIMIC-IV data.

Q1.1 ADT history

A patient’s ADT history records the time of admission, discharge, and transfer in the hospital. This figure shows the ADT history of the patient with subject_id 10001217 in the MIMIC-IV data. The x-axis is the calendar time, and the y-axis is the type of event (ADT, lab, procedure). The color of the line segment represents the care unit. The size of the line segment represents whether the care unit is an ICU/CCU. The crosses represent lab events, and the shape of the dots represents the type of procedure. The title of the figure shows the patient’s demographic information and the subtitle shows top 3 diagnoses.

Do a similar visualization for the patient with subject_id 10063848 using ggplot.

Hint: We need to pull information from data files patients.csv.gz, admissions.csv.gz, transfers.csv.gz, labevents.csv.gz, procedures_icd.csv.gz, diagnoses_icd.csv.gz, d_icd_procedures.csv.gz, and d_icd_diagnoses.csv.gz. For the big file labevents.csv.gz, use the Parquet format you generated in Homework 2. For reproducibility, make the Parquet folder labevents_pq available at the current working directory hw3, for example, by a symbolic link. Make your code reproducible.

#create a symbolic link to the Parquet folder for labevents
# ln -s ~/BIOSTAT203B/203b-hw/hw2/pq_files labevents_pq
patient_id <- 10063848

patient_data <- fread("~/mimic/hosp/patients.csv.gz") |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id) |>
  as_tibble()

admission_data <- fread("~/mimic/hosp/admissions.csv.gz") |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id) |>
  as_tibble()

patient_title = str_c("Patient ", patient_id, ", ", 
                      patient_data$gender, ", ",
                      patient_data$anchor_age, " years old, ", 
                      str_to_title(admission_data$race[1]))
transfer_data <- fread("~/mimic/hosp/transfers.csv.gz") |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id) |>
  as_tibble()
labevents <- 
  open_dataset("labevents_pq", format = "parquet") |>
  to_duckdb() |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id) |>
  collect()
procedures_icd <- 
  fread("~/mimic/hosp/procedures_icd.csv.gz") |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id) |>
  left_join(
    fread("~/mimic/hosp/d_icd_procedures.csv.gz"),
    by = c("icd_code", "icd_version")) |>
  as_tibble()
diagnoses_icd <- 
  fread("~/mimic/hosp/diagnoses_icd.csv.gz") |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id) |>
  left_join(
    fread("~/mimic/hosp/d_icd_diagnoses.csv.gz"),
    by = c("icd_code", "icd_version")
  ) |>
  as_tibble()

top3 <- diagnoses_icd |>
  group_by(icd_code, long_title) |>
  summarise(count = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(count)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  select(long_title)
`summarise()` has grouped output by 'icd_code'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.
str_top3 <- str_c(top3$long_title, collapse = "\n")
# Create the ADT history plot using ggplot2
ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = transfer_data, 
                 aes(x = intime, 
                     xend = outtime, 
                     y = "ADT", 
                     yend = "ADT",
                     color = careunit, 
                     linewidth = str_detect(careunit, "ICU|CCU"))) +
  geom_point(data = procedures_icd, 
             aes(x = chartdate, 
                 y = "Procedure", 
                 shape = str_sub(long_title, 1, 35))) +
  geom_point(data = labevents, 
             aes(x = storetime, y = "Lab"), 
             shape = "+") +
  labs(title = patient_title, 
       subtitle = str_top3, 
       x = "Calendar Time", 
       shape = "Procedure", 
       color = "Care Unit") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "1 week",
               date_labels = "%b %d") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", 
        legend.box = "vertical",
        legend.justification = "center",
        axis.title.y = element_blank()) +
    guides(linewidth = "none", 
           shape = guide_legend(ncol = 2))

Q1.2 ICU stays

ICU stays are a subset of ADT history. This figure shows the vitals of the patient 10001217 during ICU stays. The x-axis is the calendar time, and the y-axis is the value of the vital. The color of the line represents the type of vital. The facet grid shows the abbreviation of the vital and the stay ID.

Do a similar visualization for the patient 10063848.

icu_stays <- 
  fread("~/mimic/icu/icustays.csv.gz") |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id) |>
  as_tibble()
#ln -s ~/BIOSTAT203B/203b-hw/hw2/pq_chart chartevents_pq
patient_vitals <- 
  open_dataset("chartevents_pq", format = "parquet") |>
  to_duckdb() |>
  filter(subject_id == patient_id,
         itemid %in% c(220045, 220181, 
                       220179, 223761, 220210)) |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(
    fread("~/mimic/icu/d_items.csv.gz"),
    by = "itemid"
  ) |>
  print(width=Inf)

# Create the ICU vitals plot using ggplot2
ggplot(patient_vitals, 
       aes(x = charttime, y = valuenum, 
           color = label)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(abbreviation ~ stay_id, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d %H:%M") +
  labs(
    title = str_c("Patient ", patient_id, " ICU stays - Vitals")
    ) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2))

Q2.2 Summary and visualization

How many unique subject_id? Can a subject_id have multiple ICU stays? Summarize the number of ICU stays per subject_id by graphs.

icustays_tble |>
  summarise(num_subjects = n_distinct(subject_id))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  num_subjects
         <int>
1        65366
icustays_tble |>
  group_by(subject_id) |>
  summarise(num_stays = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  print(width = Inf) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = num_stays)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Number of ICU Stays per Subject ID", 
       x = "Number of ICU Stays", 
       y = "Count of Subject IDs")

Q3.2 Summary and visualization

Summarize the following information by graphics and explain any patterns you see.

  • number of admissions per patient
  • admission hour (anything unusual?)
  • admission minute (anything unusual?)
  • length of hospital stay (from admission to discharge) (anything unusual?)

According to the MIMIC-IV documentation,

All dates in the database have been shifted to protect patient confidentiality. Dates will be internally consistent for the same patient, but randomly distributed in the future. Dates of birth which occur in the present time are not true dates of birth. Furthermore, dates of birth which occur before the year 1900 occur if the patient is older than 89. In these cases, the patient’s age at their first admission has been fixed to 300.

Solution: The graph of the number of admissions per patient.

admissions_tble |>
  group_by(subject_id) |>
  summarise(num_admissions = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  count(num_admissions) |>
  print(width = Inf) |>
  
  ggplot(aes(x = num_admissions, y = n)) +
  geom_col(binwidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Number of Admissions per Patient", 
       x = "Number of Admissions", 
       y = "Count of Patients")

Majority of patients had only a few admissions, with 1 admission being the most common. There are some patients with over 12 admissions, but they are relatively rare. This is likely because most patients only require one or a few hospitalizations in their lifetime, while a smaller subset of patients may have chronic conditions or complex medical needs that require multiple hospitalizations.

The graph of the admission hour.

admissions_tble |>
  mutate(admission_hour = hour(admittime)) |>
  count(admission_hour) |>
  print(width = Inf) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = admission_hour, y = n)) +
  geom_col(binwidth = 1) +

Warning in geom_col(binwidth = 1): Ignoring unknown parameters: `binwidth`

After 12am, there is a dip in admissions, except for a spike at 7am, and then an increase after 10am. Admissions continue to rise until 4pm and stay at high levels until 12am. The spike at 7am may be due to the fact that many patients are admitted to the hospital in the morning after being evaluated in the emergency department or after being transferred from another hospital. The increase after 10am may be due to the fact that many elective surgeries and procedures are scheduled in the morning, leading to a higher number of admissions during this time. Also more accidents or emergencies are more likely to occur during daytime hours as more people are active. This may be why there is a increase from 10am to 12am, and then a dip until 7am.

The distribution of admission minute is relatively uniform, with spikes at 0, 15, 30, and 45 minutes, in decreasing magnitude. This may be due to the fact that many admissions are scheduled on the hour or at quarter-hour intervals, leading to a higher number of admissions at these times. Surgeries and other events that can be scheduled may occur at these quarter-hour or hour intervals, which leads to increased admissions at these times.

Majority of admissions have stays of less than 50 days, with a long tail of admissions with longer stays. The distribution is right-skewed, indicating that most patients have relatively short hospital stays, while a smaller number of patients have much longer stays. The long tail may be due to the fact that some patients have complex medical conditions or complications that require extended hospitalization. It is normal for patients to have shorter stays since once patients are diagnosed and stable, the system pushes to discharge.

Q4.2 Summary and visualization

Summarize variables gender and anchor_age by graphics, and explain any patterns you see.

Solution: Summarizing gender:

patients_tble |>
  count(gender) |>
  print(width = Inf) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender, y = n, fill = gender)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Gender", 
       x = "Gender (F/M)",
       y = "Count of Patients")
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  gender      n
  <chr>   <int>
1 F      191984
2 M      172643

There are more females than males in the MIMIC-IV dataset. This may be due to the fact that females tend to have longer life expectancy than males, and therefore may be more likely to be admitted to the hospital and require ICU care. Additionally, certain medical conditions that are more prevalent in females, such as autoimmune diseases and certain types of cancer, may also contribute to the higher number of female patients in the dataset.

Summarizing anchor age:

patients_tble |>
  count(anchor_age) |>
  print(width = Inf) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = anchor_age, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Anchor Age",
       x = "Anchor Age",
       y = "Count of Patients") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 5))
# A tibble: 73 × 2
   anchor_age     n
        <int> <int>
 1         18  4682
 2         19  7848
 3         20 11031
 4         21  9579
 5         22  9051
 6         23  8553
 7         24  7956
 8         25  7323
 9         26  6818
10         27  6610
# ℹ 63 more rows

There is only data of adults, ages 18 and over. There is a increase from 18-21, then a decrease until 40, where it levels off until 45. From 45-55 there is an small increase, and then a decrease until 89. At 91, there is a large spike, which is because the data counts all ages over 89 to be 91. The high frequency of patients in their 20s may be due to the fact that this age group is more likely to be admitted to the hospital for reckless and risky behavior, like driving under the influence, participating in extreme sports, and engaging in other high-risk behaviors that can lead to accidents and injuries. Additionally, this age group may also be more likely to require hospitalization for mental health issues, such as depression and anxiety, which can also contribute to the higher frequency of patients in their 20s. The decrease in frequency from ages 30-50 may be due to the fact that this age group is generally healthy and less likely to require hospitalization based on stable living. The increase in frequency from ages 45-65 may be due to the fact that this age group is more likely to develop chronic medical conditions that require hospitalization. The decrease in frequency from ages 65-89 may be due to the fact that some patients in this age group may have already passed away or may be receiving care in long-term care facilities rather than being admitted to the hospital. The spike at age 91 is due to the fact that all patients over 89 are counted as 91, which inflates the number of patients at 91 years old. Also, patients over 89 may be more likely to require hospitalization due to old-age and poor care-taking from facilities.

We are interested in the lab measurements of albumin (50862), creatinine (50912), potassium (50971), sodium (50983), chloride (50902), bicarbonate (50882), hematocrit (51221), white blood cell count (51301), and glucose (50931). Retrieve a subset of labevents.csv.gz that only containing these items for the patients in icustays_tble. Further restrict to the last available measurement (by storetime) before the ICU stay. The final labevents_tble should have one row per ICU stay and columns for each lab measurement.

Hint: Use the Parquet format you generated in Homework 2. For reproducibility, make labevents_pq folder available at the current working directory hw3, for example, by a symbolic link.

labevents_tble <- 
  open_dataset("labevents_pq", format = "parquet") |>
  to_duckdb() |>
  select(subject_id, itemid, charttime, 
         storetime, valuenum) |>
  filter(
    itemid %in% c(50862, 50912, 50971, 
                  50983, 50902, 50882, 
                  51221, 51301, 50931)
    ) |>
  left_join(
    select(icustays_tble, subject_id, stay_id, intime),
    by = "subject_id",
    copy = TRUE
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(intime), storetime < intime) |>
  group_by(subject_id, stay_id, itemid) |>
  slice_max(storetime, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(lab = case_when(
    itemid == 50862 ~ "albumin",
    itemid == 50912 ~ "creatinine",
    itemid == 50971 ~ "potassium",
    itemid == 50983 ~ "sodium",
    itemid == 50902 ~ "chloride",
    itemid == 50882 ~ "bicarbonate",
    itemid == 51221 ~ "hematocrit",
    itemid == 51301 ~ "white_blood_cell_count",
    itemid == 50931 ~ "glucose"
  )) |>
  select(subject_id, stay_id, lab, valuenum) |>
  collect() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = lab, values_from = valuenum) %>%
  relocate(sort(names(.)[-(1:2)]), .after = 2) %>%
  arrange(subject_id, stay_id) %>%
  print(width = Inf)

  filter(itemid %in% c(
    220045,
    220179,
    220180,
    223761,
    220210
    )) |>
  print(width=Inf)

clean_names <- chartitem_itemid$label |>
  str_to_lower() |>
  str_replace_all(" ", "_") |>
  str_replace_all("[^a-z0-9_]", "")

name_map <- setNames(as.character(chartitem_itemid$itemid), clean_names)
chartevents_tble <- open_dataset("chartevents_pq", format = "parquet") |>
  filter(
    itemid %in% chartitem_itemid$itemid
    ) |>
  to_duckdb() |>
  select(subject_id, stay_id, itemid,
         charttime, storetime, valuenum) |>
  left_join(
    select(icustays_tble, stay_id, intime, outtime),
    by = c("stay_id"),
    copy = TRUE
  ) |>
  filter(storetime >= intime, storetime <= outtime) |>
  group_by(subject_id, stay_id, itemid) |>
  slice_min(storetime, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    valuenum = mean(valuenum, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = itemid, values_from = valuenum) |>
  rename(!!!name_map) |>
  collect() |>
  arrange(subject_id, stay_id) %>%
  relocate(sort(names(.)[-(1:2)]), .after = 2) %>%
  print(width = Inf)

Q7. Putting things together

Let us create a tibble mimic_icu_cohort for all ICU stays, where rows are all ICU stays of adults (age at intime >= 18) and columns contain at least following variables

  • all variables in icustays_tble
  • all variables in admissions_tble
  • all variables in patients_tble
  • the last lab measurements before the ICU stay in labevents_tble
  • the first vital measurements during the ICU stay in chartevents_tble

The final mimic_icu_cohort should have one row per ICU stay and columns for each variable.

mimic_icu_cohort <- icustays_tble |>
  left_join(
    admissions_tble, 
    by = c("subject_id", "hadm_id")
    ) |>
  left_join(
    patients_tble, 
    by = "subject_id"
    ) |>
  left_join(
    labevents_tble, 
    by = c("subject_id", "stay_id")
    ) |>
  left_join(
    chartevents_tble, 
    by = c("subject_id", "stay_id")
    ) |>
  filter(anchor_age >= 18) |>
  print(width = Inf)

Q9. AI assistant

Which AI assistants (e.g., GitHub Copilot) do you use when working on this assignment? Which AI model (e.g., GPT-5 mini, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5) does the AI assistant use? How do you use them? Do you think they help improve your productivity?

Give 5 instances where AI model gave incorrect or misleading answers. You can use screenshots or copy-paste the Q&A.

I used GitHub Copilot and Claude, which ran the Claude Sonnet 4.6 Extended Model. I used Copilot while writing my code as it gave me suggestions on what to code next. I used Claude for debugging and asking it questions to understand pieces of code. They did help my productivity quite a bit. There were many times where I was stuck with errors until the model finally gave a suggestion that worked to solve the problem. 5 instances where the AI models gave incorrect or misleading answers:

  1. Copilot suggested an incorrect filter statement while reading the patients.csv.gz.

  2. Copilot suggest an incorrect pile path to reading transfers.csv.gz.

  3. Copilot suggested the wrong number of patients after I found the answer earlier.

  4. Copilot suggested selecting non-existent columns in a table.

  5. Claude intitally gave me incorrect code, the first three statements in the image. I had to then correct it by asking why it chose that order, and it listed to me its mistake and changed it to the correct order of the statements.
